claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase structure in high-entropy nanoalloys.
At elevated temperatures, nanoscale grain boundaries mediate local chemical segregation.
Surface and interface energies compete with entropy-driven mixing at elevated temperatures.
The initial nanoalloy is a disordered, single-phase material containing nanoscale grain boundaries.
Diffusion and grain-boundary effects become prominent above a critical temperature approaching a significant fraction of the melting temperature.
At moderately high temperatures, configurational entropy favors a homogeneous solid solution.
Further temperature increases enhance grain-boundary diffusion.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion causes local chemical segregation.
At sufficiently high temperatures, surface- and interface-energy contributions overcome the entropy benefit of mixing.
The competition between interfacial energetics and configurational entropy can produce nanoscale phase deviations.
High-temperature-treated nanoalloys will retain an overall single-phase structure.
High-temperature-treated nanoalloys will show more grain-boundary segregation than low-temperature-annealed samples.
High-temperature-treated nanoalloys will show greater local chemical inhomogeneity than low-temperature-annealed samples.
Below the critical temperature threshold, entropy dominates and grain-boundary effects are minimal.
The prediction is limited to temperatures high enough to activate grain-boundary diffusion but below melting or complete phase decomposition.
TEM and atom probe tomography will be used to compare phase uniformity and grain-boundary composition between otherwise identical low- and high-temperature annealing groups.
No measurable increase in grain-boundary segregation after high-temperature treatment would falsify the hypothesis.
Macroscopic phase separation after high-temperature treatment would falsify the proposed bounded mechanism.
